solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: 'King Emperor' engraved in battleship at sea in German silver (12, two words)

indicators.note: something engraved is cut into a surface, so one set of letters sits inside another
being at sea means confused and all over the place, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: Rex Imperator, the Latin title abbreviated on coins

explanation.surface: A naval scene: the monarch's title cut into a warship's silver plate while it is out at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: R.I. (Rex Imperator) appears on British coins of the George V era; it goes inside the warship's letters before they are jumbled.
explanation.definitionFit: British plate is a nickel-silver alloy, also called German silver, used as a cheap imitation of real silver.

clue.text: Wild flower causing reduction in insect numbers?

blocks.note: a fall in numbers is a loss

explanation.surface: A naturalist wonders whether some wild plant is to blame for fewer insects about.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'reduction in insect numbers' as a loss of bugs, then put the two words side by side; the question mark flags the playful split.
explanation.definitionFit: Bugloss is a bristly blue-flowered plant of the borage family that grows wild on dry ground.

clue.text: Fauvist rubbish, including exotic feast seen from below

indicators.note: in a down entry, viewing from the bottom upward reads the letters backwards
to include something is to hold it within, so one word wraps another

blocks.note: a luau is a Hawaiian feast

explanation.surface: A critic dismisses a Fauvist painting of some exotic banquet viewed from an odd angle.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hawaiian feast is turned upward, then sits inside the word for nonsense. Georges Rouault was a French painter linked with the Fauves.
explanation.definitionFit: Rouault exhibited with Matisse and the other Fauves in 1905, so a Fauvist is a fair description of him.

clue.text: What rises somewhat, clipping top of wicket?

indicators.note: clipping the top trims off the opening letter of the word that follows

blocks.note: a stump is one of the three uprights forming a cricket wicket

explanation.surface: A cricket picture: a ball that rises a little and just clips the top of the wicket.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the wicket is made of three stumps; behead one of them.
explanation.definitionFit: A tump is a dialect word for a small mound or hillock, ground that rises only slightly.

clue.text: Throws up endlessly, nursing itch alternately? It could mean day off work

definitions.text: It could mean day off work

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is dropped
taking every other letter keeps only alternate ones
to nurse something is to hold it close, so the outer word cradles the inner

blocks.note: to sky a ball is to hit it high in the air

explanation.surface: Someone vomiting and scratching an itch looks set to phone in sick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throws up' suggests vomiting, but here it means hits high in the air. A sickie is British slang for a day off claimed as sick leave.
explanation.definitionFit: A sickie is a day taken off work by pretending illness, so an absence is exactly what it signals.

clue.text: Leporine, raw, I jugged?

indicators.note: jugged means put in jug, slang for prison, so a letter is locked inside

explanation.surface: A hare speaks: raw meat now, but jugged soon, as in the classic dish jugged hare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jugged' calls up jugged hare, which suits 'Leporine', but it is the containment signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Leporine means relating to or resembling hares, which is what the rarer adjective harish also means.

clue.text: Purcell's composition about a Roman festival

indicators.note: a composition is something put together, so the letters are rearranged
going about something means surrounding it

blocks.note: the English composer's name, taken as written

explanation.surface: A music programme note: a Purcell piece written about some festival of ancient Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: The jumbled composer's name wraps the single A.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lupercal, or Lupercalia, was a February purification and fertility festival in ancient Rome.

clue.text: Hoofed animal from Italy, caught in trap, struggling

indicators.note: something caught in a trap ends up inside it
struggling thrashes about, so the letters are disordered

blocks.note: I is the international vehicle code for Italy

explanation.surface: An animal from Italy is caught in a trap and struggles to get free.
explanation.definitionFit: A tapir is a large odd-toed ungulate, so it is a hoofed mammal of the forests.

clue.text: Scots release, as of old, former member of the family?

blocks.note: eme is an old word for an uncle

explanation.surface: A Scottish question about whether some old relative has been set free.
explanation.walkthrough: Both the answer and its second piece are old or dialect words that Chambers lists.
explanation.definitionFit: Exeme is an obsolete Scots verb meaning to free or exempt, so it is an old Scottish word for release.

clue.text: Upmarket restaurateur, half cut, appearing in paper as 'Peg leg'

indicators.note: cutting in half throws away the back half of the name
to appear in something is to sit inside it

blocks.note: Bertorelli's was a well-known chain of Italian restaurants in London

explanation.surface: A restaurateur, rather drunk, turns up in a newspaper story nicknamed 'Peg leg'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half cut' suggests tipsy but means losing half the letters. Bertorelli's was a London Italian restaurant group; The Times is a British newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: Timber-toes is an old jocular nickname for a person with a wooden leg, the same as Peg leg.

clue.text: Face to windward, being connected via modem

blocks.note: dial is slang for the face
up, as in the helm put up toward the wind

explanation.surface: A sailor turns their face into the wind.
explanation.walkthrough: Dial is old British slang for a person's face.
explanation.definitionFit: Dial-up describes an internet connection made over a phone line through a modem.

clue.text: Probes former injury brought up in boasts

indicators.note: in a down entry, bringing up lifts the letters so they read from the bottom
placed inside the other word

blocks.note: to prate is to talk boastfully
tene is an obsolete word for grief or harm

explanation.surface: Someone investigating an old wound that keeps being mentioned in another's boasting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Former' marks the injury word as archaic rather than meaning ex.
explanation.definitionFit: To penetrate is to get into or through something, as a probe does when it explores.

clue.text: Coarse thread: there's adhesive holding one on page

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it within your grasp

blocks.note: p is the abbreviation for page

explanation.surface: Sticking a single thread onto a page with glue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' places the page letter after the glued unit in an across entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Guimp, or gimp, is a thick cord or thread used as trimming, with a coarser core.

clue.text: Source of hardwood? There's none on timber tree in being cut twice

indicators.note: the little word in is cut away, and the cut tree is used twice over

blocks.note: the pine is a tree grown for its timber

explanation.surface: A forester talks of a timber tree that has been felled twice and has nothing left on it.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the two letters IN out of the tree, leaving two letters, and write them twice after nought.
explanation.definitionFit: Opepe is a West African tree whose yellow timber is a durable hardwood used for piling and flooring.

clue.text: Edible fish coated in batter I almost vomit

indicators.note: almost the whole word means stopping one letter short
being coated means wrapped in an outer layer

blocks.note: to lam is to beat or thrash

explanation.surface: A diner whose fish in batter is so greasy they nearly throw up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Batter' looks like the fish coating but is the verb meaning to beat.
explanation.definitionFit: Lampuki is the Maltese name for the dolphinfish or dorado, a popular food fish there.

clue.text: Material for overalls? Search among garden implements

indicators.note: looking among the following words finds letters lying across them

explanation.surface: Hunting through the garden tools for what a gardener wears.
explanation.definitionFit: Denim is the hard-wearing cotton twill from which overalls and jeans are usually made.

clue.text: A unit at sea with mostly flat seas describing voyage?

indicators.note: being at sea means confused, so the letters are jumbled
mostly means not quite all, so the last letter goes

explanation.surface: A naval unit out on nearly calm waters, as a log of the voyage might say.
explanation.definitionFit: Nautical means relating to ships and sailing, so it is an adjective for a sea voyage.

clue.text: Choir feature in tribute to prince HM backed repeatedly

indicators.note: backed means turned to face the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a mise was a payment made to a new prince of Wales or earl of Chester
the monarch's letters used a second time

explanation.surface: A cathedral choir pays musical tribute to a prince, with the Queen in support again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: ER is the royal cipher of Queen Elizabeth; turned round and repeated it gives two syllables.
explanation.definitionFit: A miserere is a misericord, the hinged ledge on a choir stall seat that supports a standing chorister.

clue.text: Sordid stuff left inside old collar

indicators.note: inside means placed within the other word

blocks.note: an old spelling of seize, to collar or grab

explanation.surface: Something nasty left lurking inside an old shirt collar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Collar' is a verb here, to seize someone, in an archaic spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleaze is sordidness or corruption, the seedy material of scandal.

clue.text: Homeric star? I, ——, battling with arms maybe

blocks.note: first meaning: the Trojan hero of the Iliad
second meaning: the verb to bully or bluster fills the blank

explanation.walkthrough: Fill the dash with a verb: 'I bully, battling with arms maybe'. The verb comes from the swaggering image of the Trojan warrior.
explanation.definitionFit: Hector is the Trojan champion of Homer's Iliad, and to hector is to bully or intimidate with blustering talk.

clue.text: Officer in charge with future king in time of revolution?

blocks.note: OC is the military abbreviation for Officer Commanding, in charge
to-be means future, as in a bride-to-be

explanation.surface: An officer serves alongside the heir to the throne during a time of upheaval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Future king' looks like one heir, but it splits into to-be and the king's letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Russian Revolution of 1917 is known as the October Revolution, so that month is a time of revolution.

clue.text: As regards character leading regiment in War, we're concerned with breeding

definitions.note: a noun phrase in disguise: those who are concerned with breeding

indicators.note: the character that leads a word is its opening letter
placed inside the other word

blocks.note: Ares is the Greek god of war

explanation.surface: A regiment's men insist their real interest in wartime is livestock breeding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'War' stands for the Greek war god by metonymy; the regiment's first letter goes into him near the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Rearers are people who raise animals or children, so they are concerned with breeding.

clue.text: Jock's tipple supplying support around noon

indicators.note: going around something means enclosing it

blocks.note: a strut is a supporting bar

explanation.surface: A Scotsman's lunchtime drink keeps him propped up around midday.
explanation.walkthrough: Jock is a nickname for a Scot, marking a Scots word.
explanation.definitionFit: Strunt is a Scots word for spirituous liquor, so it is a Scotsman's drink.

clue.text: Called in intermediaries

indicators.note: in signals the letters lie within the next word

explanation.walkthrough: 'Called in' reads as summoning go-betweens, but 'Called' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To be termed is to be named or described as, the same as being called.

clue.text: Short extract from Oscar ceremony

indicators.note: an extract is a passage lifted out of a longer text

explanation.surface: A brief clip taken from the Academy Awards show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short extract' looks like a film clip; 'Short' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Short in the sense of in short supply means scarce, lacking enough.

clue.text: Pigment is seen when climbing over Sicilian location

indicators.note: in a down entry, climbing means reading from the bottom up

blocks.note: Enna is a town in central Sicily

explanation.surface: A colour seen by a climber looking down over a Sicilian hill town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' places the turned-round word above the town in a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Sienna is an earth pigment, raw or burnt, named after the Italian city of Siena.

clue.text: Fail through nerves, changing title in computer program (8, two words)

indicators.note: changing the word alters the order of its letters
placed inside the other word

blocks.note: a bot is an automated program

explanation.surface: A nervous coder fails when renaming something in a piece of software.
explanation.walkthrough: To bottle it is British slang for losing your nerve at the crucial moment.
explanation.definitionFit: Bottle is British slang for courage, so to bottle it is to back out through lack of nerve.

clue.text: Prohibition disheartened aestheticist in military district

indicators.note: losing the heart strips the middle, leaving only the two ends

explanation.surface: An aesthete is downcast by a ban imposed within an army district.
explanation.definitionFit: The Banat was a frontier region of Hungary, organised as a military district against the Ottomans.

clue.text: Foreign lingo for rainy day, yielding odd characters

indicators.note: giving up the odd-numbered letters keeps only the even ones

blocks.note: second, fourth, sixth letters and so on

explanation.surface: Learning a foreign language as something saved up for a rainy day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yielding' means surrendering here: the odd letters are given up, not produced.
explanation.definitionFit: Oriya, now Odia, is the Indian language of Odisha, a foreign tongue to a British solver.

clue.text: It's dry round core of pot for perennial

indicators.note: the core is the very centre, so the middle letter is kept
going round means surrounding

explanation.surface: Advice that a pot plant is dry around its roots.
explanation.definitionFit: An aroid is a plant of the arum family, such as cuckoo-pint, typically a perennial.

clue.text: Attorney General's aide corrected most of error involving Latin

indicators.note: most of a word is all but its last letter
correcting changes things around, so the letters are rearranged
involving means wrapping up inside

blocks.note: Lat is the abbreviation for Latin

explanation.surface: A law officer's assistant fixes a mistake in the Latin of a document.
explanation.definitionFit: A relator is a person who brings information on which the Attorney General starts a legal action.

clue.text: Guinness, say, something served in pubs cold

blocks.note: C for cold on a tap

explanation.surface: Guinness, the stout served cold in pubs.
explanation.walkthrough: Guinness looks like the drink, but it is the actor Sir Alec Guinness.
explanation.definitionFit: Alec is the forename of the actor Guinness, so it is an example given by 'say'.

clue.text: Priest's daughter, extremely fussy about eulogy's opening

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter
about in the sense of all around, so the outer word encircles the single letter

explanation.surface: A priest's daughter is very particular about how his funeral tribute begins.
explanation.walkthrough: Nice in its old sense means fastidious; 'extremely' just intensifies that.
explanation.definitionFit: Niece was a polite euphemism for the illegitimate daughter of a Catholic priest or pope.

clue.text: Old clod confined to single bed

indicators.note: letters confined to the words that follow lie inside them

explanation.surface: An old oaf is restricted to sleeping in a single bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old clod' reads as a dull old man, but it is an archaic word for a lump of earth.
explanation.definitionFit: Glebe is an old poetic word for a clod of earth or soil, as well as church land.

clue.text: Rarely used net from class abandoned us in rough sea

indicators.note: abandoned means left behind, so those two letters are dropped from the word
a rough sea is churned up, so the letters are mixed
placed inside the other word

blocks.note: a genus is a class in biology

explanation.surface: A fishing net, hardly ever used, from a group that deserted us in a stormy sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A sagene is a rare word for a fishing net, closely related to seine.

clue.text: Strippers jiggling breast with candle

indicators.note: jiggling shakes things about so the letters fall out of order

explanation.surface: Exotic dancers shimmying with candles, a racy nightclub act.
explanation.definitionFit: Table dancers perform erotic dances, often stripping, close to customers' tables in clubs.
